p: Um, how, how does the time frames as far as a turnover difference in those causes?
So for lead and asbestos, about 4 to 6 months of abatement work depending on how many components in the apartment test positive.
And can you share a workflow of how units get ready after vacancy, uh, after vacancy with the Committee?

Sure, we can follow up with your office and share some of that information, but again, uh, residents typically spend about 27 years in an apartment, so upon turnover there's significant skilled trades work that needs to get done. We typically remove all of the cabinets, we do plumbing work and upgrades, we do plastering and then painting of the apartment, and that all happens after the abatement for both lead and asbestos.
And what's the average cost, uh, of making a vacant unit move-in ready?
So the average cost is about $40,000, and that includes the environmental work.
And, uh, with NYCHA's outstanding need for capital improvement being, uh, large, uh, do you have an estimate of how many additional revenue NYCHA would take in from the activation of the 6,000 units?
I don't have that number with, uh, with me today, but we can—

Can you get that to us, please? Uh, do you have an estimate of the impact, uh, that additional revenue would have on the funding, on funding key safety and well-being improvements such as the Hud pillar areas like lead and mold?
Again, we can follow up once we've determined what that resident del— that revenue rather, uh, is.

Okay, and what steps is NYCHA taking, uh, to ensure property security for these vacant units? I know that's been something of a concern, um, and frustration by residents who occupy

units near those particular vacant apartments. Um, so what steps have been taken, uh, where squatters or non-residents, uh, may be in danger for lawful residents in the developments?

Thank you, Council Member. It's a frustration for our property management staff as well. No one is happy about, uh, a squatter coming into our development. Uh, but we're happy to report that we've had a very good working relationship with both DOI and NYPD on our Housing Bureau reclamation work. And so since the start of that work in 2023, we've recovered over 630 apartments in conjunction with the NYPD and DOI. And most of that work starts from a property management report of, uh, or a resident report of someone maybe being in a unit that is not authorized to be in that unit. And so property staff takes that information to the law department, and we work closely with NYPD and DOI to investigate whether the people in that unit are authorized to be in that unit or not, and, or not. And then we follow up with the NYPD to reclaim the unit.
So is there an active list of those units that, uh, occupied that?

There's obviously a list that we're currently working on, but there— we don't have a full list of every squatter condition, but we encourage residents to report that. We have an anonymous tip line that they can report that to if they don't feel safe reporting it directly to property management.
Well, you just said that the management staff is working actively to identify those particular units.
Yes.
I mean, they obviously have—
As I said, we have a list that we're working on, but if we don't, there's obviously some that maybe we don't know about, and we'd encourage residents to report that to us.
So you're saying that there are some units that you don't know of that, uh, that, that have squatters in them?
Of course, yes. I can't possibly— we don't possibly know everything that's going on. When we're told or when we find out about squatters in a unit, we start to take actions, but I don't know.

So how often are y'all checking on these units for security purposes? Uh, it goes back to securing them. Uh, how, how often? What does that look like? Is there a constant check on those units, uh, that are vacant?

Yes, thank you, Council Member. So we do— we, we started to do annual inspections on all vacant units that are as part of our annual inspections of all units. In addition, vacant units do have many workers coming through as part of the turnover process. And as part of the DOI report that just came out, we did agree to do monthly vacant unit inspections as well.
And when do you plan to start that?
We've, uh, we are working on some technology upgrades in order to track that work and I can get back to you with the timing.

Well, I just wanna make— hopefully it's, it's an urgent response because obviously, uh, having a vacant unit and having someone, you know, a squatter in there, uh, we've heard a host of security issues and concerns that are coming from the residents. So I'm hoping that NYCHA

moves forward with securing those particular units. Um, when it— I think the, uh, Chair of the Finance Committee touched on federal funding risk, um, particularly, uh, funding for the Emergency Housing Voucher program provided by HUD, which provides assistance to about 5,500 households in this— in our city, and is set to expire come this November of this year. Do you have any updates on the status of the funding for this program?

Thank you for that question. Uh, as you know, EHV was originally funded through 2030, um, but a change was announced in March of 2025 saying that the funding would sunset at the end of 2026. Continuing rental assistance for the EHV households is a priority for NYCHA, and we are currently evaluating alternative options. But there is currently insufficient funding for those households.
Have you been working with the Administration to find, uh, other programs, uh, that these households might qualify for?
Of course.
Okay and what is the total annual cost for these families to maintain their housing?
$124 million.

$124 million. I guess we'll move on to now evictions, uh, an Office of Impartial Hearings. Um, the Office of Impartial Hearings, uh, within NYCHA oversees hearings and grievances between tenants and the authority. Uh, does the Office of Impartial Hearings also oversee the disputes between tenants and PACT developers as well?
No, they do not.
Who oversees those disputes?
Oh, is it— no, he asked for
You want to repeat the question?
No.
Okay.
Uh, OIH, uh, handles disputes between NYCHA and our tenants. They do not handle disputes between PACT partners and tenants. It would be Housing Court. OIH is different than Housing.

But I'm asking you who oversees, like, who— I believe, is it NYCHA responsible for, uh, intervening in, in controversies or disputes that may come up with tenants and the, uh, developer or management company?
So I, I think— I'm not sure I understand your question. So if you could clarify it, that would be—

So— I'll ask the question again. Maybe that may bring some clarity. Uh, since the Office of Impartial Hearings within NYCHA oversees hearings and grievances between tenants and the authority, does the Office of Impartial Hearings oversee disputes between the tenants and PACT developers? And if not, who does?
So the answer is no.
Okay.

And If there are disputes that need to be adjudicated, that would be done in housing court. If there are disputes that, uh, a, a tenant brings to our attention, we routinely meet with our PACT partners, our tenants, as, uh, Jonathan said earlier. Um, people can call 311, they can call the CCC, they can call the ombuds person depending on the

issue, but if you're talking about the adjudication, that would be in Housing Court.
Okay, so how many complaints or disputes come about, uh, that are reported to NYCHA for PACT?

I don't have a total number, uh, because we have— as we have described throughout this hearing, there are many venues for which complaints come through, uh, whether it's directly through the PACT partner or from residents, rather, directly to us, whether it's from Council Members, uh, residents directly have a lot of our numbers. So we don't have an aggregate number.

Okay, so I guess this is— this question will matter. Can you share information about the number of hearings per month or a year, that outcomes— their outcomes, and any trends in evictions you are seeing?
This question is regarding OIH, correct?
Correct.

Okay, at any given time, the Office of Impartial Hearing has approximately 750 active matters. Um, in addition to conducting

hearings, OIH handles a variety of other administrative responsibilities. In 2025, the OIH scheduled over 1,300 cases for hearings, issued over 2,000 decisions stemming from hearings, default, and other applications, and scheduled or facilitated over 1,300 Right-to-Counsel conferences.
And, and, and, and these are eviction, uh, disputes?
No, they're all types of hearings, so -
Okay, but particularly for eviction disputes, can you give us the numbers on that?
That is, uh, information that I don't have in front of me but I can get that for you.

I would like for you to provide that for this Committee, please. During a PACT conversion process, Section 8 developers can choose, uh, to forgive or collect rental arrears. Am I correct? Uh, and if chosen, a portion of those collected arrears are intended to go to Section 9. Am I correct? Is that—
Uh, well, we sell the arrears at the closing, so they pay us for arrears. So I'll let the CFO explain how that benefits—

Let me just give some context. Uh, in a hearing we had a couple of months back in the, uh, pre— previous session of the Council, it was stated that, uh, if there are arrears during the conversion, uh, that the management company can either forgive or the new owners or developers. They can either forgive or they can either, uh, they can either collect those arrears. Uhm, and then we was told that there's also deals that are made with NYCHA that can be made with NYCHA, and NYCHA can get a percentage of those arrears. Is that still the case?

That is correct. So there are two things that happen, prior to the conversion as a part of the closing deal, we determine how much, you know, the PACT developer will pay us for arrears. We have a general rule that we don't take less than 80 cents on every dollar of arrears owed. After the closing, the developer can decide from their perspective whether or not they want to forgive

the arrears, keep the arrears, partially forgive, but that is independent of the funds that NYCHA receives.
Okay and which developments have those agreements, uh, been agreed to and how much of that has been collected?
Every development at the time of conversion, we decide what to do with the arrears. And as a part of the deal documents, they have to pay us at closing.
So every development-
That has converted through—
That has converted has made an agreement?
Correct.
Okay and, uh, who oversees the collection and the distribution of those arrears?
The collection is overseen by the Finance Department, it;s treated like any other receivable.
And do we know how much has been collected?
We can get that number for you.

Okay. Uh, obviously when we're talking about, um, uh, revenue generation, generating revenue for the authority when it comes out of commercial space rental. Uh, how many commercial space vacancies exist within NYCHA's portfolio?
Thank you for that question. We have 70 total commercial spaces. 60 are occupied, 10 are vacant, the total gross rent roll for 2026 as of March 23rd is $4,192,208.34.
Do you have a, uh, do you have a plan to fill those vacancies?
Yes.
Does that mean the authority's in the-
Yes, of course.
And what's the plan?
The plan is we're looking for a tenant that can pay us rent. So as with every other vacant commercial space, we have a team that's currently working on trying to fill those vacancies.

Are these units also in disrepair as well? I mean are these particular

spaces in disrepair, and is there some type of plan or program to repair them if that's the case?
Um, I'm not sure what this, these vacant spaces look like. We can certainly get back to you. I would assume that—
But I would be happy to get a plan on it.
They would have to be built up. or built out.

That would be part of the plan to have that assessment made, right? If you're gonna rent them. Okay, alright. Do you have a sense of, um, how much revenue could be generated? I think I had asked that earlier. To support the critical infrastructure needs of, uh, Section 9 developments through the renting of these space— of these spaces?

Uh, I do not, but I feel pretty confident to say that the— these 10 vacant units are not going to substantially impact the $80 billion need that we have. Of course, we always want to generate revenue.
That would be a plus.
Of course, of course.
So I think for NYCHA residents, uh, they would, they would like those, uh, those commercial spaces rented, so.
Correct.

Okay, is there any opportunity for these commercial spaces to support NYCHA resident pop-ups or small business owners living in NYCHA developments? This is part of the plan. I'm trying to help you give you ideas on how to put this plan together.
There are many options but that could be part of the plan.

Okay, uh, actually, another question that will help you formulate this plan that you have already. Uh, have you explored the idea of working with social services, uh, community-based organizations to provide programming such as workforce development, counseling, cultural enrichment opportunities for these spaces?
We have many other spaces, our community centers, and I can turn it over to our—
No, I'm not talking about the community centers, I'm talking about these, the-
The 10 vacant spaces.
In your plan that you have.
If there's community service providers can pay us rent, then we are open to, uh, including them in our plan.
Okay, well, we look forward to seeing your plan once you create the plan, okay?
Perfect.

We look forward to it. Thank you. And now we, we now move to, uh, the second round of questioning, and, uh, we have, uh, Council Member Mealy who has joined us, and, uh, we'll obviously get the opportunity to ask questions. Council Member Mealy.

Thank you, Chair. I had a quick question. Thank you. Um, the prime— Preliminary Financial Plan for Fiscal 2026 and '30 includes Fiscal Budget, um, 2027 —up $375.9 million for NYCHA pass-through expense funding, unchanged from the amount budgeted in November. The city's share of NYCHA Fiscal Budget in the Preliminary Budget was $103— $103 less. So could you explain that in regards to the fiscal budget going forward in November to the current one in 2027?
Thank you, Council Member Mealy, for that question.
Is it $15 million less?

So I, I don't know what particular numbers you're referring to, but I will say that there are discrepancies between the NYCHA adopted budget, which was passed in November of 2025, and the city's preliminary plan, which was recently released. So NYCHA only releases one budget a year, um, and so in 2025, in November, when we adopt our budget with our board, we include the city sources at that time. As we, of course, manage through the year, we do have conversations with City Hall and OMB to ensure that we are using the funds that are added for us appropriately. But we only pass one budget a year, so you won't see adds in a formal adopted budget from the prior months.
Okay, I'm sorry that I was late. I'm upstairs. Could you go over how many vacancies you still have left? You said it's 70. Could you go over that again, please?
In what kind of vacancy, ma'am?
Um, uh, vacancies, commercial space.
Thank you for that question. We have a total of 70 commercial spaces. 60 are occupied and 10 are vacant.
10 are vacant. Is that— do you know how many vacancies in NYCHA that are vacant on the first and second floor?
I believe all of our commercial spaces are on the first floor, but we can check that and get back to you.

No, because, um, I'm just noticing since the City of Yes, all of a sudden I've counted at least about 10 NYCHA developments that have mysteriously— a first floor is vacant, the second floor is vacant. With City of Yes, it can be commercial on the first and second floors. So I was just wondering how many of your NYCHA developments that have the first and second floor vacant, could you please give us an update on that? 'Cause that is not something I'm just saying. It's true.

Thank you for that question. We will check to see where our 10

vacancies are located, and we will break it down between first floor and second floor.

Okay then. Could you, um, give me— how much revenue are you getting from Amazon with those boxes? I never saw a hearing on it, but I see at NYCHA you have those Amazon boxes. So what kind of revenue are you getting from them?
Thank you, Council Member. We can follow up with you on the exact amount, but we, um, we—
How long they've been there? You should know about how much you're making off of them, right?
Yes, I'm sorry, I just don't have that information with us today, but we, uh, we do work closely with resident leaders to place those lockers.
Oh, the resident leaders knew about-
Yes, we-
You all went to them.

Yes, every time we're considering a resident locker, we walk the development with the

resident leader to confirm the placement and to confirm that there's—
And some of them did not want it, it was only the resident leader that made that decision?

Resident leader with their board, yes. But we're happy to report that we've, um, we have over 1,000 individual lockers installed across 130 developments. We've had over a million packages delivered through those lockers, and it's really increased the safety and security, both preventing thefts and, uh, of packages.
So you don't know how much you are making now because you are helping Amazon, are you not?
We do have a contract where Amazon pays us a certain amount.
How much was the contract?
Per month for each locker? I, it could be 50 to 100 per box.
50 to 100 a box?
Per box, depending on the development.
You could have got more. Is there any other outside vendors that you're making extra money off?
We have a variety—
And should any of that funding go to the TA presidents?
